dedupe_keys.name: qzss satellite report for disaster and crisis management dc report in japan

description: This operations and emergency-response case covers the use of Japan's Quasi-Zenith Satellite System (QZSS) to broadcast disaster information from space. The DC Report service sends short messages on the L1S signal, shared with the sub-metre augmentation service, every four seconds; content includes earthquake and tsunami information from the Japan Meteorological Agency, converted to a compact format and also shared on social media. From 1 April 2024 an extended service (DCX) began carrying J-Alert messages, such as missile launch warnings, and L-Alert evacuation instructions, and adopted a common alert message format; distribution of alerts for Asia-Pacific partners was under study for launch from fiscal 2025. The service is meant for receivers on powered outdoor equipment such as streetlights and signage, and on vehicles such as car navigation systems, so that warnings reach people where terrestrial networks are down. Test messages go out around the fourth Thursday of each month, and independent users have documented reception on commercial receivers such as u-blox modules. Coverage: Japan, with signal footprint over South-East Asia and Oceania. Format and access: service overview, notices and interface specifications (IS-QZSS-DCR and DCX) from the Cabinet Office, free. Caveats: few public figures on real-world receivers in use or on alerts delivered; documentation of actual events is limited. Simulation uses: emergency communication redundancy when mobile and broadcast networks fail, and design of warning dissemination chains. Related records: Galileo's emergency warning service is the European counterpart, and the Japanese ministry's 2011 telecom damage record shows why redundancy is needed.
